triage.name: Animal Bites
triage.reason: A bite wound is a concrete presentation requiring history of the animal, exam for tendon/nerve/joint involvement, and decisions on antibiotics, rabies and tetanus.

demographics: Dog bites are the most common animal bite overall and occur at all ages
Cat bites are more common in adult women and older adults
Children are bitten most often on the face, head and neck because they are at the animal's level
Adults are bitten most often on the hands, arms and legs
Bites from wild or exotic animals are more common in people with occupational or recreational animal contact

risk_factors.text: Owning or frequently handling dogs or cats
Young child left unsupervised around a pet
Occupational animal contact (veterinarian, animal control, farm work, wildlife handling)
Unfamiliar or stray animal, or animal that is sick, injured or protecting food or young
Alcohol or recreational drug use around animals
Immunosuppression or diabetes (raises infection risk after a bite)

comorbidities: Immunosuppression (including asplenia, HIV, transplant, chronic steroids)
Lymphedema or prior mastectomy on the affected side
social_history: Pet ownership or household with dogs or cats
Outdoor or rural work and recreation
exposures: Rodent, rabbit or other small mammal bite
Wild animal bite (raccoon, skunk, fox, bat, monkey)

chief_complaints.text: My arm is sore and swollen where the animal bit me
The wound is red and draining

hpi.onset: Sudden, at the time of the bite; most patients present within hours to a day, though some wait until the wound becomes infected
hpi.duration: Usually less than 24 hours at presentation; infected bites may present after 1–3 days
hpi.progression: Immediate pain and bleeding at the bite site, followed by swelling and tenderness; if infection develops, redness, warmth, increasing pain and purulent drainage appear over 12–72 hours
hpi.location: Depends on the animal and situation: hands, forearms and legs in adults; face, scalp and neck in children
hpi.radiation: Pain is usually local; deep bites near a joint or nerve can cause shooting pain or numbness in the distribution of the affected nerve
hpi.quality: Sharp, stinging or aching pain; crushing pain with large dogs
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; severe with deep puncture wounds, fractures or tendon injury
hpi.timing: Constant, worse with movement of the affected part
aggravating: Moving the affected hand, arm or leg

associated_symptoms.text: Bleeding from the wound at the time of the bite
Swelling and tenderness around the wound
Numbness or tingling beyond the wound (possible nerve injury)
Inability to fully move a finger or the hand (possible tendon injury)
Fever and chills if the wound becomes infected
Red streaks spreading up the limb

pertinent_negatives: Bite from a bat, raccoon, skunk, fox or other high-risk rabies animal
Unprovoked attack by a healthy-appearing animal
Loss of consciousness or head injury during the attack
Heavy bleeding that will not stop
Fever at the time of the bite (suggests pre-existing infection rather than a fresh bite)
Known bleeding disorder or use of anticoagulants
Tetanus vaccination more than 5–10 years ago

positives.text: Feeling warm or feverish if the wound is infected
Break in the skin, puncture marks or a laceration
Redness, warmth and swelling around the wound
Pus or cloudy drainage from the wound

negatives: Skin ulcers unrelated to the bite
argues_against: A spreading rash suggesting cellulitis from another cause
A chronic ulcer suggesting vascular or diabetic wound

positives.text: Pain with movement of the affected hand, arm or leg
Weakness or inability to move a finger or joint
Numbness or tingling in the fingers or toes beyond the wound

negatives: Weakness on one side of the body
argues_against: Head injury with altered mental status
Anaphylaxis from venom or drug reaction

positives.text: Anxiety or fear after the attack

atypical.how_it_differs: Bites are more often on the face, scalp and neck because children are at the animal's level; they may not report the bite or may be frightened and give a limited history.
Thinner skin and poorer circulation mean bites tear more easily and become infected with less obvious redness, swelling or fever.
Infection can develop rapidly and spread deeply with less pain and fewer local signs; unusual organisms are more likely.
Neuropathy and poor perfusion can mask pain and delay healing, so the wound may look minor while infection is deep.
Presentation is similar, but antibiotic and imaging choices must be adjusted for fetal safety.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, holding the injured part still
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, guarding the injured limb, but not toxic-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, in obvious pain, may be pale or diaphoretic
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or agitated, signs of shock or spreading infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the wound under good light, measuring its length and depth
findings.finding: Puncture marks, laceration or avulsion with surrounding bruising

findings.maneuver: Palpate the wound edges and surrounding tissue
findings.finding: Focal tenderness and swelling around the bite

findings.maneuver: Inspect and feel the skin around the wound
findings.finding: Erythema, warmth and induration extending from the wound

findings.maneuver: Inspect the limb proximal to the wound
findings.finding: Red streaks tracking up the limb

findings.maneuver: Palpate the draining lymph node basin
Ask the patient to flex and extend each finger and the wrist against resistance
findings.finding: Inability to flex or extend a finger or joint, suggesting tendon injury

findings.maneuver: Test two-point discrimination and light touch distal to the wound
findings.finding: Decreased sensation in the distribution of a nerve crossing the wound

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently move the adjacent joint
findings.finding: Joint effusion, pain with passive motion or a wound communicating with the joint

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the limb for deformity or crepitus
findings.finding: Deformity, abnormal motion or crepitus suggesting fracture

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial or dorsalis pedis pulse distal to the wound
Press the nail bed and observe refill
findings.finding: Delayed capillary refill distal to the wound

findings.maneuver: Document intact sensation, motor function and distal pulses
findings.finding: Intact sensation, full motor function and palpable distal pulses

findings.maneuver: Explore the wound with a gloved finger or probe when safe
findings.finding: No retained tooth fragment, dirt or foreign body

findings.maneuver: Observe the wound after applying direct pressure
findings.finding: Bleeding controlled with pressure, no pulsatile or persistent bleeding

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude infection, especially early or in older or immunocompromised patients.
Supports the diagnosis of wound infection but does not identify the organism.
Elevated only with severe or systemic infection such as sepsis.
Prolonged only if the patient is anticoagulated or has a bleeding disorder; not a routine test for a bite.
Elevated only with anticoagulation or coagulopathy.
Consider only with extensive crush injury or compartment syndrome.
Negative. Ordered in anyone who could be pregnant before radiographs, sedation or antibiotics that are unsafe in pregnancy.

imaging.study: X-ray of the affected part (hand, forearm, leg or skull)
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected fracture, retained tooth fragment or foreign body, or deep puncture over bone

findings.text: Retained radiopaque tooth fragment or foreign body
Soft tissue swelling around the wound

imaging.study: CT of the affected region with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected deep space infection, abscess, osteomyelitis or retained foreign body not seen on x-ray

findings.text: Soft tissue abscess or fluid collection
Deep soft tissue swelling and fat stranding
Foreign body or retained tooth fragment

imaging.study: MRI of the affected region without and with contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected tendon, joint or bone involvement, or when CT is nondiagnostic
Children and pregnancy when a retained foreign body is suspected and radiation should be avoided

findings.text: Retained foreign body or tooth fragment
Soft tissue fluid collection or abscess

initial.why: White count and differential support wound infection and assess for systemic illness
Baseline renal function and electrolytes before antibiotics or surgery

initial.test: X-ray of the affected part (hand, forearm, leg or skull)
initial.why: Looks for fracture, retained tooth fragment or foreign body
initial.only_if: suspected fracture, deep puncture over bone, or retained foreign body

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before radiographs or antibiotics that are unsafe in pregnancy

confirmatory.why: Identifies the causative organism and guides antibiotic choice in infected or deep bites

confirmatory.test: CT of the affected region with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Defines deep space infection, abscess or osteomyelitis
confirmatory.only_if: suspected deep infection, abscess or retained foreign body not seen on x-ray

supporting.why: Adds to the white count in assessing the severity of wound infection
Supports the diagnosis of deep or bone infection
Assesses for sepsis in a toxic-appearing patient
supporting.only_if: systemic illness or sepsis is suspected

supporting.test: MRI of the affected region without and with contrast
supporting.why: Best test for tendon, joint or bone involvement
supporting.only_if: suspected tendon, joint or bone injury, or CT is nondiagnostic
child or pregnant patient with suspected retained foreign body

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of a bite wound
Not needed unless the presentation suggests pancreatitis
Not part of acute bite evaluation; may be checked later if diabetes is suspected
Not routine; reserved for suspected deep infection or retained foreign body
not_indicated.only_if: suspected deep infection, abscess or retained foreign body not seen on x-ray

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected tendon, joint or bone involvement
not_indicated.only_if: suspected tendon, joint or bone injury, or CT is nondiagnostic

decision_points: Assess tetanus vaccination status and give a booster or immunoglobulin as indicated
Assess rabies risk based on the animal species, behavior and availability for observation or testing; start post-exposure prophylaxis when indicated
Examine for tendon, nerve, joint and bone involvement before closing the wound
Do not close cat bites or infected wounds primarily; leave them open or loosely approximated
Start antibiotics for infected bites, deep puncture wounds, hand or face bites, and immunocompromised or diabetic patients
Pregnancy test before radiographs or antibiotics that are unsafe in pregnancy

differential.name: Human bite (clenched-fist injury)
differential.why_considered: A wound over the knuckles or hand that looks like an animal bite but the history involves striking a person in the mouth
differential.trigger: Wound over the metacarpophalangeal joints in a patient who punched someone in the mouth

history: Punched or struck another person in the mouth
Wound noted after a fight, sometimes with a delayed or vague account
Alcohol or drug use around the time of injury
exam: Small puncture or laceration over the third or fourth metacarpophalangeal joint
Wound may look minor but extends into the joint or tendon sheath
Pain and swelling that worsen when the hand is flexed
labs: Wound culture grows oral flora including Eikenella corrodens
imaging: X-ray for fracture, retained tooth fragment or foreign body
MRI or CT if deep space infection or septic arthritis is suspected

differential.name: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
differential.why_considered: A bite wound with rapidly worsening pain, swelling and systemic illness
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to the wound, skin discoloration, crepitus or rapid progression over hours

history: Pain worsening much faster than expected for a simple bite
Rapidly spreading redness or skin discoloration
Diabetes or immunosuppression
exam: Pain out of proportion to the visible wound
Tense swelling, bullae, dusky or necrotic skin
Crepitus or loss of sensation over the affected area
Systemic toxicity with tachycardia and hypotension
imaging: CT showing gas in soft tissues, fat stranding or fluid collections

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Redness, warmth and swelling around a wound, with or without a clear bite history

history: Spreading redness and warmth over hours to days
Often no clear break in the skin or a minor one
Fever and chills
exam: Diffuse erythema, warmth and induration without a deep puncture
Tender regional lymph nodes
No tendon, nerve or joint deficit
imaging: Not usually needed; ultrasound or CT if an abscess is suspected

differential.name: Abscess
differential.why_considered: A fluctuant, painful swelling at or near the bite site

history: Increasing focal pain and swelling days after the bite
Fever and malaise
exam: Fluctuant, tender mass
Overlying erythema and warmth
Purulent drainage if it ruptures
imaging: CT showing a rim-enhancing fluid collection

differential.name: Tendon laceration or tenosynovitis
differential.why_considered: A deep bite over the hand or wrist with inability to move a finger

history: Bite over the dorsum of the hand or wrist
Inability to flex or extend a finger after the injury
Pain with finger movement
exam: Weakness or absence of flexion or extension of a finger
Tenderness along the tendon sheath
Fusiform swelling of the finger with it held in slight flexion
imaging: MRI showing tendon discontinuity or fluid in the tendon sheath
Ultrasound showing tendon injury or sheath fluid

differential.name: Septic arthritis
differential.why_considered: A bite near a joint with a swollen, painful joint

history: Bite directly over or near a joint
Joint pain and swelling that worsen over hours to days
Fever
exam: Joint effusion, warmth and pain with passive motion
Wound communicating with the joint space
Inability to bear weight or move the joint
labs: Joint aspirate with high white count and positive Gram stain or culture
imaging: MRI showing joint effusion and bone marrow edema

differential.name: Osteomyelitis
differential.why_considered: A deep bite over bone with persistent pain and fever

history: Deep puncture wound over a bone
Persistent pain and fever despite wound care
Diabetes or immunosuppression
exam: Focal bone tenderness
Overlying swelling and erythema
Wound that fails to heal or drains
imaging: X-ray showing bone destruction or periosteal reaction (often late)
MRI showing bone marrow edema and enhancement

differential.name: Foreign body reaction
differential.why_considered: A bite wound that remains painful and swollen with a retained tooth fragment or debris

history: Persistent pain and swelling after the bite
Wound that does not heal or drains intermittently
History of a deep puncture
exam: Focal tenderness and induration
Wound may drain or have a visible fragment
No tendon or nerve deficit
imaging: X-ray showing a radiopaque tooth fragment or foreign body
Ultrasound showing a retained foreign body
CT showing a retained fragment and surrounding inflammation

severity.mild: Superficial abrasion or small laceration, no deep structures involved, no signs of infection, patient comfortable
severity.moderate: Deep puncture or laceration with local swelling and tenderness, early signs of infection such as erythema and warmth, but no systemic illness
severity.severe: Deep wound with tendon, nerve, joint or bone involvement, or established infection with fever, purulent drainage and regional lymphadenopathy
severity.critical: Rapidly progressive infection with sepsis, necrotizing soft tissue infection, compartment syndrome, or major hemorrhage from a large vessel injury

red_flags.finding: Pain out of proportion to the wound or rapidly spreading redness
red_flags.meaning: Possible necrotizing soft tissue infection; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis; needs resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Inability to flex or extend a finger or joint
Numbness or tingling beyond the wound
red_flags.meaning: Nerve injury; needs careful documentation and possible surgical repair

red_flags.finding: Wound over a joint with swelling and pain on passive motion
red_flags.meaning: Possible septic arthritis; needs joint aspiration and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Bite from a bat, raccoon, skunk, fox or other high-risk rabies animal
Tetanus vaccination not up to date

red_flags.meaning: Possible major vessel injury; needs urgent surgical evaluation

complications.name: Wound infection
clues: Increasing pain, redness and swelling 12–72 hours after the bite

complications.name: Tendon laceration or tenosynovitis
clues: Inability to flex or extend a finger

complications.name: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
clues: Pain out of proportion to the wound

complications.name: Rabies
clues: Progressive encephalitis with hydrophobia, agitation and confusion

special_populations.differences: Bites are more often on the face, scalp and neck; they may not report the bite or give a limited history. Facial bites need careful cosmetic and functional assessment.
Thinner skin and poorer circulation mean bites tear more easily and become infected with less obvious redness, swelling or fever.
Infection can develop rapidly and spread deeply with less pain and fewer local signs; unusual organisms are more likely. Lower threshold for antibiotics and close follow-up.
Neuropathy and poor perfusion can mask pain and delay healing, so the wound may look minor while infection is deep. Higher risk of osteomyelitis.
Presentation is similar, but antibiotic and imaging choices must be adjusted for fetal safety. Avoid radiographs when possible and choose pregnancy-safe antibiotics.

key_questions.question: What kind of animal bit you, and do you know the animal or was it a stray?
key_questions.looking_for: Species and ownership; a known, healthy, owned dog or cat can be observed, while a stray or wild animal raises rabies risk

key_questions.question: Was the attack provoked or unprovoked?
key_questions.looking_for: An unprovoked attack by a healthy-appearing animal is a rabies red flag and changes post-exposure prophylaxis decisions

key_questions.question: When exactly did the bite happen?
key_questions.looking_for: Time since injury; most present within hours, but a delay of 1–3 days suggests developing infection

key_questions.question: Where on your body is the wound, and how deep does it look?
key_questions.looking_for: Hand, wrist, face or joint-adjacent wounds carry higher risk of deep structure injury and infection

key_questions.question: Can you move all your fingers, hand or toes normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to flex or extend suggests tendon injury and needs surgical evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you have any numbness or tingling beyond the wound?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensory loss in a nerve distribution suggests nerve injury

key_questions.question: Is the wound getting more painful, red, swollen or draining?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive local signs over 12–72 hours suggest wound infection or abscess

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms suggest infection, sepsis or a deeper process

key_questions.question: When was your last tetanus booster?
key_questions.looking_for: A booster more than 5–10 years ago, or an unknown status, requires tetanus prophylaxis

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, HIV, or take any medicines that suppress your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression or diabetes lowers the threshold for antibiotics and close follow-up

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood thinners or do you have a bleeding disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulation or coagulopathy increases bleeding risk and may change wound management

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy affects radiograph and antibiotic choices

key_questions.question: Do you have any allergies to antibiotics, especially penicillin or cephalosporins?
key_questions.looking_for: Guides antibiotic selection for bite prophylaxis or treatment

key_questions.question: What is your job or hobby — do you work with animals or handle wildlife?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or recreational animal contact raises exposure risk and may affect rabies assessment

reasoning_points: A clear history of a bite from a dog, cat or other mammal with a break in the skin
Wound inspection showing puncture marks, laceration or avulsion with surrounding tenderness and swelling
Assessment for deep structure injury: tendon function, sensation, joint involvement and possible fracture
Evaluation for local infection with erythema, warmth, purulent drainage or regional lymphadenopathy
Tetanus vaccination status reviewed and prophylaxis given when not up to date
Rabies risk assessed from the animal species, behavior and availability for observation or testing
Antibiotic decisions based on wound type, location, depth and patient risk factors
Imaging and cultures used selectively for suspected fracture, retained foreign body or deep infection

easy: Known healthy pet dog or cat with a superficial laceration and a clear bite history
Patient presents within hours with pain and bleeding but no signs of infection
Tetanus status is up to date and rabies risk is low
Wound is on the forearm or leg and does not involve deep structures
medium: Cat bite puncture wound over the hand with early redness and swelling
Patient with diabetes or immunosuppression and a bite that looks minor
Wound over a joint or tendon with pain but preserved function
Delayed presentation 2–3 days after the bite with purulent drainage
hard: Deep hand bite with inability to flex a finger, suggesting tendon injury
Bite from a stray or wild animal with unclear rabies vaccination status
Older adult with thin skin and minimal signs despite a deep infection
Child with a facial bite requiring cosmetic and functional assessment
Rapidly worsening pain and swelling suggesting necrotizing soft tissue infection
